text: Multiple chores combined into one request.
Retrieve a specific medical item (e.g., EpiPen, inhaler, ice pack, heating pad).
Operate a household fire extinguisher (pull pin, aim, squeeze, sweep).
Skim foam or fat off the top of a boiling liquid.
Extinguish a small stovetop grease fire (e.g., by covering it with a lid or baking soda, never water).

Kids: bedtime routine (bath-water temperature check, pajamas, story, night light, checking on a sleeping child), bottle and formula prep, sterilizing, supervised play (catch, hide-and-seek, card and board games), reading aloud.

section: Reaching, climbing, and fixing. Tool handling stops at basic hand tools, and there's no height access.
text: Small plumbing and fixes: unclog sinks and shower drains, fix a running toilet, reset a garbage disposal, clear a printer jam, bleed a radiator.
Food safety: avoid cross-contamination (raw-meat boards, hands), control allergens (read labels, clean shared tools), discard food left out too long.
Diets and planning: halal, kosher, vegan, gluten-free, low-sodium, diabetic, texture-modified; meal planning; scaling recipes; baby food.

Technique: carve, fillet, shuck; awkward produce (squash, pineapple, mango, coconut); baking steps (grease and line pans, proof dough, cool on racks, frost); grilling (light, flip, check temperature, propane level); disposing of cooking oil; espresso with steamed milk, pour-over.

Situational variations. Apartments and condos (elevators, shared laundry, HOA rules), regional standards (metric vs. imperial, front vs. top-load, induction vs. gas, shoes-off homes), languages, accents, and speech differences, residents with disabilities or dementia, residents' emotional states, and robot-side degradation (dirty camera, low battery, network down, a failing arm).
“Deal with this mess.” It has to inspect the situation and create its own cleanup plan.
“Finish whatever I forgot to do.” It needs to inspect the environment and infer incomplete chores.
“Check whether I left anything out.” Requires understanding what the expected household state normally looks like.
“Check the house before we leave.” It has to inspect locks, windows, appliances, pets, lights, faucets, garage doors, and other household-specific concerns.
“Get the house ready for bed.” It must combine locking doors, dimming lights, closing blinds, checking appliances, preparing rooms, and possibly pet routines.
“Get the house ready for the morning.” It might prepare coffee equipment, bags, clothes, lunch items, blinds, and room temperature.
“Bring in the groceries, but take the frozen stuff first.” Requires prioritizing temperature-sensitive items.
“Put away the groceries properly.” It may encounter unfamiliar food and must infer pantry, refrigerator, freezer, or countertop storage.
“Figure out where this new kitchen gadget should go.” Requires estimating frequency of use, size, compatibility with existing organization, and available space.
“Make more room in the refrigerator.” Requires rearranging containers while considering temperature zones, spills, expiration, and food safety.
“Use these leftovers before they go bad.” Requires inspecting ingredients, judging compatible combinations, and planning a meal.
“Make dinner with whatever we have.” One of the hardest: identify ingredients, possible dishes, missing substitutes, preparation order, and dietary constraints.
“Make something similar to what we ate yesterday.” Requires episodic memory and approximation.
“Make enough food for whoever is here.” Requires estimating portions dynamically.
“Make this recipe even though we’re missing one ingredient.” Requires substitution reasoning.
“Make this less salty.” Requires corrective cooking reasoning.
“Save this dish; I messed it up.” Requires diagnosing what went wrong and identifying possible recovery actions.
“Figure out why the floor is wet.” Could be spilled water, a leak, pet water, rain, appliance overflow, etc.
“Something is leaking. Find it.” Requires tracing evidence to a source.
“There’s a weird noise somewhere.” Requires localization, appliance knowledge, and anomaly detection.
“Get the usual.” Requires learning routines and preferences.
“Figure out why this appliance isn’t turning on.” Requires safe diagnostic reasoning while knowing when not to proceed.
“Do it without waking anyone up.” Requires reasoning about doors, floors, lights, vacuum noise, dishes, etc.
“Clean while people are still using the kitchen.” Requires dynamically working around moving humans and active tasks.
“Wait until I’m done with that.” Requires recognizing task dependencies.

“Optimize the house for low energy today.” Requires reasoning across multiple systems: lowering the thermostat, closing blinds facing the sun, turning off vampire-draw electronics, and delaying the dishwasher until off-peak hours.
“Make a meal using only ingredients that expire this week.” Combines inventory scanning, expiration date reading, and recipe generation on the fly.
“Something’s burning!” Requires locating the source, then choosing between cutting power or gas, smothering, evacuating, or calling for help in seconds.
“The power just went out.” Requires working out what matters right now: light, fridge, medical devices, kids, phones.
“Is that pan still hot?” / “Is this safe to stand on?” Requires inferring temperature or stability before touching.
“Something fell behind the fridge.” Requires retrieving it without moving the appliance.
“This lid’s stuck.” / “This window won’t open.” Requires loosening it without breaking it (heat, tapping, leverage, grip).
“I’ve had a rough day.” Requires choosing between quiet, dinner, tea, or leaving them alone.
